title: Statement on Inclusive and Sustainable Artificial Intelligence for People and the Planet (Paris AI Action Summit)
issuer: French Presidency of the AI Action Summit and participating States
reason: Official Élysée page and PDF read. The statement is a non-binding political declaration adopted on 11 February 2025; the official page lists 65 endorsers (63 States, the EU and the African Union Commission), while the PDF lists 64 and a contemporaneous Canadian release listed 60. The discrepancy is recorded in the instrument record.
evidence: Official Élysée English page, official 3-page PDF (SHA-256 9a19a426c0d1ffdcd2dab40340074663ca4e8ff3eaeb1c3d1d2067e3fd9a2c64), and the Government of Canada's contemporaneous release.
gaps: Endorser list inconsistent across official publications (60/64/65); no depositary or update log; US and UK did not endorse.

title: AI Impact Summit Declaration, New Delhi (New Delhi Declaration on AI Impact)
issuer: Government of India and participating States and international organisations
reason: Official Ministry of External Affairs text and Press Information Bureau release read. A non-binding declaration adopted on 19 February 2026 and endorsed by 92 countries and international organisations; the PIB annex itemises 90 States, the EU and IFAD as of 5 March 2026, while the MEA page lists 91 and omits Colombia. The fourth summit in the Bletchley-Seoul-Paris series; added after the summit-series audit found it missing from the corpus.
evidence: Official MEA declaration text; PIB release with the 92-name annex (as of 5 March 2026, https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2231208&reg=3&lang=1); official AI Impact Summit outcome page.
gaps: The MEA page lists 91 and omits Colombia while the PIB annex lists 92; the discrepancy is unexplained; no follow-up mechanism verified; the count includes the EU and IFAD.

title: BRICS Leaders' Statement on the Global Governance of Artificial Intelligence
issuer: BRICS Leaders, 17th BRICS Summit, Rio de Janeiro
reason: Official BRICS Presidency PDF and Brazilian Ministry of Foreign Affairs page read. The first stand-alone BRICS leaders' statement on global AI governance, adopted on 6 July 2025; non-binding and without an individual signature block. The presidency's list of 11 member States is recorded as a collective issue, not as individual signatures. Added after the audit of other international AI instruments.
evidence: Official BRICS Presidency PDF of the statement; Brazilian MFA page confirming the date and the 17th BRICS Summit setting.
gaps: No individual signature block; 11 member States are listed, not individually evidenced issuers; Saudi status contested; no follow-up mechanism; relationship to WAICO not formal. The full English text is stored and segmented.

title: Global AI Governance Initiative
issuer: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the People's Republic of China
reason: Official MFA English text and Chinese original located. A unilateral Chinese government proposal for international AI governance, issued on 18 October 2023; non-binding and with no formal adherence list. It is the principal documented Chinese-pole instrument and is included as a non-binding principles document, not as an agreed international instrument.
evidence: Official MFA English text (stored HTML, SHA-256 073933c76fa44d0cf1f30d1cbe95b17ad6a625f29abd12024e3550f2adde5b59) and the Cyberspace Administration of China original.
gaps: No endorsement list; the 2025 Global AI Governance Action Plan is not separately catalogued; only the English translation is stored.

title: Collaboration on the safety of AI: UK-US memorandum of understanding
issuer: United Kingdom and United States
reason: Official GOV.UK publication and press release read. Bilateral MOU signed on 1 April 2024 by Michelle Donelan and Gina Raimondo; non-binding; implemented by the UK and US AI Safety Institutes. GOV.UK publishes a summary of key elements, not the full MOU, so the record is metadata-only.
evidence: Official GOV.UK publication (2 April 2024) and press release; signature by the UK Secretary of State for Science, Innovation and Technology and the US Secretary of Commerce; no full MOU text linked.
gaps: Full MOU text not published; the summary states no duration, termination, review or dispute-settlement procedure.

title: Joint Statement EU-US Trade and Technology Council of 4-5 April 2024 (AI Safety Dialogue commitment)
issuer: European Union and United States
reason: Official European Commission and USTR joint statement read. The AI section records a commitment by the European AI Office and the US AI Safety Institute to establish a Dialogue; it is a political commitment in a broader joint statement, not a standalone MOU, administrative arrangement or binding agreement.
evidence: European Commission and USTR joint statement, 5 April 2024; NIST and European Commission pages on the first technical Dialogue, 11 July 2024; no standalone terms of reference located.
gaps: No standalone US–EU AI-safety MOU or administrative arrangement located; the commitment creates no binding obligations.

title: International AI Safety Report
issuer: International expert panel chaired by Yoshua Bengio, commissioned by the AI Seoul Summit
reason: Authoritative international scientific report, not an instrument creating obligations. It is a candidate for the 'authoritative materials' layer, but its 2025 and later editions were not verified on an official source in this session.
evidence: Discovery only.
gaps: Official publication URL, date and editions need verification.

title: CCW Group of Governmental Experts on Emerging Technologies in the Area of Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems
issuer: UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons
reason: The principal multilateral military-AI negotiating track. Its 2024–2026 final report (CCW/GGE.1/2026/3, adopted 4 September 2026) sets out elements of an instrument and other measures. The Seventh Review Conference endorsed them and continued the GGE with a mandate to elaborate an instrument, without prejudging its nature, and to recommend its legal form, including a binding protocol.
evidence: Official UNODA GGE meeting page, final report CCW/GGE.1/2026/3, and the Seventh Review Conference final document CCW/CONF.VII/CRP.1/Rev.3 (20 November 2026) read.
gaps: No adopted instrument or draft protocol; the 2026 report is not a treaty text. First 2027 sessions scheduled 1–5 March and 30 August–3 September 2027.

title: Recommendation CM/Rec(2020)1 of the Committee of Ministers on the human rights impacts of algorithmic systems
issuer: Council of Europe Committee of Ministers
reason: The official Recommendation PDF and the Council of Europe news release were read. It is an AI-specific, non-binding Recommendation addressed to the 47 member States, adopted on 8 April 2020, with no signature, ratification or depositary. It is included as a distinct Council of Europe standard-setting text, not as a treaty.
evidence: Official PDF of CM/Rec(2020)1 with the guidelines; Council of Europe news release of 8 April 2020; adoption at the 1373rd meeting of the Ministers’ Deputies.
gaps: Non-binding. No itemised endorsement list exists because it is addressed to all 47 member States. Full text stored and segmented; national implementation is not assessed.

title: ITU-T Recommendation Y.3172: Architectural framework for machine learning in future networks including IMT-2020
issuer: International Telecommunication Union
reason: Official ITU-T recommendation page and database record read. Recommendation ITU-T Y.3172 (06/2019) was approved on 22 June 2019, is in force, belongs to the Y.3000-Y.3499 series and is maintained by ITU-T Study Group 13. It is an international technical recommendation, not law, and is catalogued at metadata level in the standards layer.
evidence: ITU-T recommendation page (approval date 2019-06-22, status in force, free English PDF and EPUB); ITU-T recommendation database record (AAP, Study Group 13, handle.itu.int/11.1002/1000/13894).
gaps: Non-binding technical recommendation. Full text not acquired; national implementation not assessed.

title: IEEE 7000-2021: Standard Model Process for Addressing Ethical Concerns during System Design
issuer: IEEE Standards Association
reason: Official IEEE SA standard page and launch notice read. IEEE 7000-2021 is an active standard published on 15 September 2021 (Board approval 16 June 2021; PAR approval 30 June 2016), issued by C/S2ESC with working group EMELC-WG and available free through the IEEE GET Program. It is a general systems-engineering standard, not AI-specific, and is catalogued at metadata level in the standards layer.
evidence: IEEE SA standard page (status Active Standard, published 2021-09-15, committee C/S2ESC, free access through the IEEE GET Program); IEEE SA news release of 15 September 2021.
gaps: Not AI-specific. Non-binding technical standard; full text not acquired; certification and organisational use not assessed.

title: CEN-CENELEC Joint Technical Committee 21 on Artificial Intelligence
issuer: CEN and CENELEC
reason: Verified but not catalogued as an instrument: JTC 21 is a standardisation committee, not a standard, declaration or treaty. The official CEN-CENELEC pages record that it was established on 1 June 2021, unites over 300 experts from more than 20 countries, works through five working groups and develops harmonised standards in support of the EU AI Act under standardisation request M/593, as amended by M/613. Its published output is catalogued separately: EN 18286:2026 (record `cen-en-18286-2026`), cited in OJ L 2026/2274.
evidence: CEN-CENELEC Artificial Intelligence topic page (establishment, experts, working groups, M/593); CEN project page for EN 18286:2026 (work item JT021039, Published, M/613, OJ L 2026/2274); CEN-CENELEC news of 23 October 2025 on acceleration measures and of 28 October 2026 on the revised deadline.
gaps: The committee is not an instrument. Its other work items (for example prEN 18228, prEN 18283 and prEN 18285) are drafts and are not catalogued individually; national adoption is not assessed.

issuer: G7 (2023 Japanese Presidency)
reason: Companion to the catalogued Hiroshima Process Code of Conduct. It is a distinct non-binding document and should be added as a separate record once its text is acquired.
evidence: Listed on the official MIC Hiroshima AI Process documents page.
gaps: Full text not acquired; relationship to the Code to be documented.

title: Hiroshima AI Process Reporting Framework
issuer: G7 / OECD
reason: Implementation and reporting mechanism for the Hiroshima Process Code of Conduct, launched 7 February 2025 and hosted by the OECD. It is implementation material, distinct from the Code, and was not verified in detail.
evidence: Official Hiroshima AI Process reporting page and OECD publication located.
gaps: Questionnaire, participation data and legal nature need verification.

title: ISO/IEC 23053:2022 Framework for Artificial Intelligence (AI) Systems Using Machine Learning (ML)
issuer: ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 42
reason: International technical standard closely related to ISO/IEC 22989. Its individual ISO catalogue record was verified and it is catalogued as a technical standard.
evidence: Listed in the ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 42 catalogue.
gaps: Individual catalogue page, exact status and price need verification.

gaps: A full-text AI keyword check was not performed; exclusion is provisional.

issuer: CPTPP Parties
reason: A major digital-trade treaty, but no express AI-specific provision was located in its full English text. It is not included in the AI-provisions category; it remains relevant as general digital-trade background.

gaps: A full-text AI keyword check was not performed; exclusion is provisional.

reason: A large regional trade agreement; no express AI-specific provision was located in the materials consulted. Outside the core AI-provisions category.

issuer: United Nations

title: Agreement on the Establishment of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO)
issuer: Founding States of WAICO; China is the depositary and host
reason: Official MFA signing and ratification statements, the Xinhua report of the NPC ratification decision, the October 2026 MFA progress report, the 31 July 2026 MFA account and the Indonesian government's list of the 29 initial signatories were read. The Agreement is a treaty establishing an independent intergovernmental international organization with international legal personality, subject to ratification and not in force. The record is included as a separate AI-specific treaty, not as a political declaration.
evidence: MFA English signing article; MFA spokesperson statement of 9 November 2026; Xinhua report of the NPC Standing Committee decision of 6 November 2026; MFA progress report of October 2026 (29 plus 9 equals 38, but only four of the nine are named there); MFA account of 31 July 2026 naming eight additional signatories; Indonesian government list of the 29 initial signatories; Digital Watch reproduction of the Agreement text.
gaps: The MFA reports 38 founding members, while the October progress report says nine States joined after the initial 29 and the 31 July account names eight of them; the ninth is unnamed. China's NPC approved ratification but no deposit was verified; the Agreement is not in force. The official Chinese text is stored and segmented; no depositary register or notification was located.

title: Pax Silica Declaration
issuer: Pax Silica Summit participants, convened by the United States Department of State
reason: Official State Department and Australian government publications were read. The Declaration is a non-binding political declaration on secure AI and technology supply chains, with 26 signatories (25 States and the EU) as of 23 October 2026. It is included as the US-led architecture cited in the three-pole analysis and as a distinct instrument from the 2023 military-AI declaration.
evidence: State Department Pax Silica page with the declaration text and partner list; State Department 26 June 2026 fact sheet (24 signatories including the United States); State Department 23 October 2026 release (Paraguay as 26th signatory); Australian government publication of the 12 December 2025 declaration (seven founding signatories); State Department Taiwan joint statement (non-signatory participant).
gaps: Non-binding. The State Department partner list omits the United States, whose signature is confirmed by other official sources. Taiwan is a non-signatory participant. The separate AI Opportunity Statement (54 endorsers) is not catalogued here.

title: Implications of artificial intelligence for the promotion and protection of human rights (A/HRC/RES/63/15)
issuer: United Nations Human Rights Council, 63rd session
reason: Official A/HRC/RES/63/15 read in full. Adopted without a vote on 6 October 2026; a dedicated Human Rights Council resolution applying international human-rights law across the AI life cycle. Added after the coverage checklist identified the HRC layer as missing from the corpus.
evidence: Official English PDF A/HRC/RES/63/15 (6 pages, read in full); UN Digital Library record; summary record A/HRC/63/SR.41. Adopted without a vote, 41st meeting, 6 October 2026.
gaps: Non-binding; no vote or signatory list; no enforcement; only English read; full text stored and segmented into 24 units.

title: G7 Digital and Technology Ministerial Declaration: 29 May 2026
issuer: G7 Digital and Technology Ministers (France presidency)
reason: Official GOV.UK text read in full and adoption confirmed by the Japanese MIC and the French presidency. The declaration has express, substantive AI provisions in two of its four priorities (secure AI and AI adoption) and therefore meets the inclusion rule; it is catalogued as a non-binding political declaration, not as an AI-specific treaty or as Hiroshima Process implementation material.
evidence: Official GOV.UK publication of the English text, agreed in Paris on 29 May 2026 and published 1 June 2026; Japanese MIC results page of 1 June 2026 confirming adoption as the ministerial's outcome document; French presidency release of 29 May 2026.
gaps: Broad digital/tech scope; only the AI-related sections are recorded; the referred G7 deliverables and the revised Reporting Framework are not analysed individually.

title: G20 AI Prosperity Compact (2026)
issuer: G20 Innovation Ministers, Chapel Hill, 2 September 2026

It is excluded from the catalogue because it creates no State-level commitment and is not a public-law text; the separate G20 AI Prosperity Objectives are catalogued as the ministerial deliverable.
evidence: US Department of Commerce G20 Innovation Ministerial pages; White House release of 2 September 2026 describing the Compact as a private-sector partnership pledge.
gaps: Not an intergovernmental instrument; no State signatures, ratifications or depositary. Excluded by design.

title: Paris Call for AI Safety and Security
issuer: Governments, AI companies and civil-society organisations, convened by the President of France
reason: A multi-stakeholder voluntary declaration, not an intergovernmental instrument. The Élysée page lists 19 governments alongside 11 companies and 11 civil-society organisations, and the list remains open to new endorsements. It is excluded from the instrument corpus but recorded as a political call; it may be relevant to an authoritative-materials layer.
evidence: Official Élysée page, posted 9 November 2026, with the text and a signatory list that is updated as new endorsements arrive; the page lists governments, companies and civil society, not States alone.
gaps: Not an intergovernmental instrument; no treaty, ratification, depositary or enforcement; signatory list changes; the US is not a signatory.

title: G20 Innovation Ministerial Statement: 2 September 2026
issuer: G20 Innovation Ministers, Chapel Hill, United States
reason: A broad innovation ministerial statement across six pillars. AI is one pillar, but the text is not AI-specific and does not create legal obligations; the separate G20 AI Prosperity Compact and Objectives are pending as their own candidate. Excluded as a general innovation statement.
evidence: Official GOV.UK publication of the statement agreed in North Carolina on 2 September 2026; White House release describing six pillars, including AI.
gaps: Broad innovation scope; AI-specific G20 deliverables are pending; no legal obligation.

title: Arab Convention on Combating Information Technology Offences (2010)
issuer: League of Arab States
reason: UNODC records adoption on 21 December 2010 and entry into force on 7 February 2014 after seven instruments; the English text reproduction confirms the treaty structure, criminal-law provisions and LAS depositary. It is included as a binding regional cybercrime treaty. The current party table could not be read, so no current party count is asserted.
evidence: UNODC pre-ratification compendium (adoption, entry into force, seven-State threshold, LAS membership); English text reproduction (final clauses and substantive provisions); attempted LAS depositary page.
gaps: The LAS depositary table was unreachable, so current Parties, reservations and declarations are not verified. The English working text is an AsianLaws reproduction, not an official LAS translation; the official Arabic PDF is stored but not segmented. No map.

title: CIS Agreement on Cooperation in Combating IT Crimes (2018)
issuer: Council of Heads of State of the Commonwealth of Independent States
reason: The CIS Executive Committee document page records signature at Dushanbe on 28 September 2018 and status “in force”; the Russian Foreign Ministry treaty entry confirms entry into force on 12 March 2020 and for Russia on 17 July 2022. It is a binding regional cybercrime treaty and replaces the 2001 CIS agreement between its Parties. It is included; the party list is declared by a Russian legal register, not by an itemised depositary table, so it is not mapped.
evidence: CIS Executive Committee document page and register; Russian Foreign Ministry treaty entry; Russian legal register listing seven Parties and Russia’s reservation.
gaps: The depositary does not publish a current party table; the seven-State list is declared by a secondary register. The official Russian text is stored and segmented; no English text was acquired. No map.

issuer: ECOWAS Council of Ministers
reason: The official signed English text records adoption by the ECOWAS Council of Ministers at Abuja on 19 August 2011, publication in the Community Official Journal and implementation by 1 January 2014. It is binding ECOWAS community law addressed to Member States, not an international treaty; it is included under the regional_law category so the cyber layer is not reduced to treaties and EU law.
evidence: Official signed English text (Articles 34–35 on publication and implementation); AfricanLII consolidation recording publication on 19 August 2011.
gaps: Binding internal community law, not an international instrument; excluded from the international-binding set. The official English scanned text is stored and OCR-segmented; national implementation is not assessed. No map.

The text is an adopted AI-specific ministerial deliverable, non-binding and without signature or depositary; it is included as a distinct record. The companion AI Prosperity Compact is a private-sector pledge and is excluded.

title: CIS Agreement on Cooperation in Combating Offences relating to Computer Information (Minsk, 2001)
issuer: Council of Heads of State of the Commonwealth of Independent States
reason: The CIS Executive Committee confirms signature at Minsk on 1 June 2001 and status “in force”; the UNODC compendium factsheet records entry into force on 14 March 2002, three instruments required, and explains that the 2018 Dushanbe Agreement replaces it only between its Parties. It is the first regional cybercrime treaty and remains the applicable CIS instrument for States that have not joined the 2018 Agreement. Included as a binding cyber treaty; the depositary does not publish a current party table.
evidence: CIS Executive Committee document page; UNODC pre-ratification compendium factsheet; English translation of the Agreement.
gaps: Current party count and the States for which the Minsk Agreement remains in force are not verified. The stored English translation is segmented; the authentic Russian text was not acquired. No map.

title: SCO Agreement on Cooperation in Ensuring International Information Security (2009)
issuer: Governments of the Member States of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization
reason: The SCO official document page and text, the UNODC compendium factsheet and the Hong Kong Treaty Series confirm the 2009 Agreement, its four-notification entry-into-force clause and its coverage of cybercrime as one of the information-security threats. It is a binding regional treaty missing from the corpus and is included. The UNODC factsheet gives 16 June 2009 as the entry-into-force date, but Article 12 and the treaty-series record give 2 June 2011; the record notes the conflict.
evidence: SCO official document page and English text; UNODC compendium factsheet; Hong Kong Treaty Series entry; national ratification records.
gaps: Current party list, including accessions by later SCO members, is not published. The official English text is stored and segmented; the authentic Russian and Chinese texts were not acquired. No map.
